videos.script:
Everything so far has been values you made up inside the program. Real work starts when the data is on disk — and the first thing to notice is that its shape is not yours. {{shape}} Somebody else chose the columns, the encoding and where the commas went, and your program has to meet it where it is.

{{three}} Three things stand between a file and a Python value, and this lesson is those three.

{{with}} First, opening it. `open` gives you a file object and you must close it — and the way you close it is by not writing `close` at all. `with open(...) as f:` closes it on the way out, including when the line inside raises. That is lesson 8's `finally`, written for you, and it is why every example in this lesson uses it.

{{encoding}} Second, the encoding. A file on disk is bytes; a string in Python is text; something has to say which bytes mean which characters. **Write `encoding="utf-8"` every time.** Left out, Python uses whatever the machine's default is — which is UTF-8 on your laptop and something else on the server, and the failure is a `UnicodeDecodeError` naming a byte, on a file that reads perfectly here.

{{format}} Third, the format. JSON and CSV both have libraries in the standard library, and you will be tempted to skip them — JSON looks like a dictionary, CSV looks like `split(",")`. It is not. A comma inside a quoted field, a newline inside a value, a `null`, a number that is a string: each of those is a bug in the hand-written version and a non-event in the library one.

{{theirs}} And the half that is really about other people's data: what arrives is never quite what the documentation said. A key missing, a `null` where a list was promised, a single object where you expected an array of them. There is a section on reading data you did not produce, and it is the difference between a script that works on the sample and one that runs on Monday.

{{binary}} Finally, bytes — for the case where the file is not text at all, and for the one line that tells you when you need them.

One CSV, read three ways. Six lines, three columns: name, city, score.

{{by-hand}} First, by hand. Open the file, split each line on the comma, take the pieces. It works, and I have written this a hundred times.

{{comma}} Now I add one row: a city written `"Porto, Portugal"` — quoted, with a comma in it. The hand-written version splits it into four pieces and puts `Portugal"` in the score column. It does not raise. The total at the end is wrong, and nothing anywhere says so.

{{reader}} Second, `csv.reader`. The same file, and the quoted comma stays inside its field, because the reader knows the format has quoting in it. Three lines shorter, too. But I am still saying `row[2]` and remembering that 2 is the score.

{{dict}} Third, `csv.DictReader`. It takes the header row and hands me a dictionary per row — `row["score"]`, by name. Now a column inserted in the middle of the file breaks nothing, and the code says what it means.

{{numbers}} One thing all three share and it is worth saying out loud: every value comes out a STRING. `row["score"]` is `"91"`, not 91, and `sum` over those is a `TypeError` — or worse, a concatenation. Converting is your job, and it is the line where a bad row will announce itself.

{{point}} Three versions, one file. The first is the one that is wrong and does not say so.

Use `with`, name the encoding, and let a library parse the format.

{{with}} Every file you open goes in a `with`. It is shorter than remembering `close`, and it closes the file when the line inside raises — which is the case nobody tests and everybody eventually hits.

{{encoding}} `encoding="utf-8"` in every `open` and every `read_text`. The default is the machine's, the machines differ, and the failure arrives on the one you cannot debug.

{{iterate}} To read a large file, iterate the file object. `for line in f:` reads one line at a time, so a four-gigabyte file costs you one line of memory — and `f.read()` costs you four gigabytes.

{{library}} `json` and `csv` are in the standard library. Use them. A JSON writer you wrote yourself will escape a quote wrongly on the day the data contains one, and a CSV you built by joining commas is broken the first time a value has a comma in it.

{{theirs}} And for data that is not yours: `get` with a default, check the type before you index, and let the row that makes no sense name itself in the error. **A file is a promise somebody else made** — read it as though they meant it and handle it as though they did not.
